THE CITY THAT CHANGED THE CURRENT

Why Chicago
Reversed Its River.

Same river. A different direction.
A remarkable response to a drinking-water crisis.

Change the year. Watch the water. ↓
Direction of flow

Before 1900 — the river carries water toward Lake Michigan.

Schematic, not a navigation map. The framing stays fixed; the arrows show the change. The fountain pin marks today’s location, not a feature present in 1900.

01

THE ORIGINAL CURRENT

A river to the lake.

The Chicago River naturally flowed into Lake Michigan. As the city grew, sewage and industrial waste followed that same route.

02

THE DRINKING-WATER PROBLEM

Too close for comfort.

Lake Michigan was also Chicago’s source of drinking water. Sending the city’s waste toward the lake put that supply at risk.

03

THE ENGINEERING ANSWER

Turn the current around.

The Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal opened in 1900. It drew the river away from the lake, toward the Des Plaines River and, farther downstream, the Illinois and Mississippi.

A BIG CHANGE. AN UNFINISHED JOB.

Moving water wasn’t the end of the story.

The reversal protected Chicago’s lake water by sending pollution downstream. Wastewater treatment and continuing investment in water quality became essential parts of the district’s work.

BACK TO THE FOUNTAIN

One hundred years.
One very fitting fountain.

Established in 1889, the water district marked its centennial with this fountain in 1989. The arc and cascades turn an enormous engineering story into something you can pause beside—and sometimes feel as a little river mist.
